domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: Keynote traces AI coding-model evolution (Sonnet 3.5 tool-call era, Opus 4.5 long-running tasks, Mythos orchestration) and argues software engineers must abandon skeuomorphic habits and build wider product spectra.

summary: Theo Browne opens the AIEWF2026 closing keynote by describing his 'AI psychosis'—disorientation from rapid model evolution. He frames three model eras: Sonnet 3.5 as the tool-call era (first reliable in-context tool calls for daily coding), Opus 4.5 as enabling hours-long autonomous task completion with self-verification, and Mythos as orchestration—a model understanding both the codebase and itself, capable of spawning sub-models and decomposing work without custom tooling. His central thesis: since models improve faster than humans, engineers must 'go bigger' rather than merely get better. He admits he was wrong about models hitting a wall. Using iOS 7's abandonment of skeuomorphism as analogy, he argues developers cling to legacy tools—terminals, Vim, Git conventions, language identities—that prioritize familiarity over utility, challenging sacred cows like why env files can't be committed or why engineers qualify themselves by language. He then presents three personal project tiers: a Reddit meme scraper (side project), Ping/Zoom for streamers (startup, YC), and a full-stack cloud platform ('too big'). These tiers have shifted downward: former startups are now side projects, and many conference attendees' entire products could be markdown files. He demonstrates this with a PR triage service he replaced with a markdown file on a cron job that runs at 9 a.m. and generates his daily work priorities. With the 'too big' tier now undefined—he doesn't know what too big means anymore—Browne pivots from 'bigger' to 'wider.' He introduces a breadth-versus-depth framework: Vercel chose depth in front-end deployment while AWS covers breadth. Previously, small teams couldn't match large competitors' breadth, but AI agents now make breadth viable—you can build a database platform in a day or two. The key strategic insight is architecting for user-driven extensibility: build enough across a spectrum to let users start, and when they need features in a vertical you don't support, they build it themselves—like Slack accidentally became an agent platform. Browne closes by challenging the audience: it's time to compete with Slack, AWS, and Salesforce directly. If your idea doesn't feel stupid, it's not big enough.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and AI psychosis
sections.summary: Theo Browne introduces himself as a YouTuber keynoting at AIEWF2026 and asks the audience about their experience of 'AI psychosis,' promising to induce it by talk's end.

sections.title: Model evolution: Sonnet 3.5, Opus 4.5, and Mythos
sections.summary: Browne traces three model eras: Sonnet 3.5 as the tool-call era (first reliable tool calls for daily coding), Opus 4.5 enabling hours-long autonomous task completion, and Mythos as orchestration—understanding itself, spawning sub-models, decomposing work without custom tooling.

sections.title: The imperative to go bigger
sections.summary: Browne argues that since models are improving faster than humans, engineers must go bigger rather than get better. He admits he was wrong about models hitting a wall and notes his previous work was too small to benefit from Mythos.

sections.title: Skeuomorphism and the iOS 7 analogy
sections.summary: Using iOS 6 vs iOS 7 compass design, Browne illustrates how skeuomorphism (mimicking physical tools) gave way to utility-first design once adoption was won. He argues developers are in their own skeuomorphic phase, clinging to terminals and familiar tools over useful ones.

sections.title: Challenging legacy developer habits
sections.summary: Browne challenges specific sacred cows: terminal as interface, Git's inability to commit env files, language-based developer identity, sunk-cost attachment to code, and the practice of 'guilt merging' suboptimal PRs out of interpersonal discomfort.

sections.title: Personal projects and the tier shift
sections.summary: Browne presents three personal projects as tiers—Reddit scraper (side project), Ping/Zoom for streamers (startup, YC), and a full-stack cloud platform (too big)—and concludes that with bigger models, everything has shifted one tier lower.

sections.title: The markdown file tier and the 'too big' gap
sections.summary: Browne introduces the 'G brain tier'—products that are just markdown files. He shares his PR triage service replaced by a markdown file on a cron job. He then identifies a gap: the 'too big' tier is now undefined. He doesn't know what too big means anymore—training models, building operating systems, competing with NPM?—and finds this both scary and exciting, pushing him to find the limits.

sections.title: Thinking wider: breadth vs depth and user-driven extensibility
sections.summary: Browne pivots from 'bigger' to 'wider,' introducing a breadth-versus-depth framework. Vercel chose depth in front-end; AWS covers breadth. Previously small teams couldn't match breadth, but AI now makes it viable. He advocates architecting for user-driven extensibility—building enough across a spectrum so users can build missing features themselves, as Slack accidentally enabled. He closes challenging the audience to compete with Slack, AWS, and Salesforce: if your idea doesn't feel stupid, it's not big enough.
